q.t: Whose assassination on 28 June 1914 set off the chain of events leading to the First World War?
q.e: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated. This set off a chain of events leading to the First World War (1914-18).

q.t: Which TWO of these countries fought as part of the Central Powers in the First World War?
q.e: The Allies fought against the Central Powers, mainly Germany, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, the Ottoman Empire and later Bulgaria. Britain was part of the Allied Powers, which included France, Russia, Japan, Belgium and Serbia.

q.t: Roughly how many Indians fought on behalf of Britain in the First World War, and how many were killed?
q.e: The whole of the British Empire was involved in the conflict. For example, more than a million Indians fought on behalf of Britain in lots of different countries, and around 40,000 were killed.
o: More than a million fought and around 40,000 were killed
More than 40,000 fought and around 1,000 were killed
More than a million fought and around 400,000 were killed
More than 60,000 fought and around 40,000 were killed

q.t: About how many British casualties were there on the first day of the British attack on the Somme in July 1916?
q.e: Millions of people were killed or wounded, with more than 2 million British casualties. One battle, the British attack on the Somme in July 1916, resulted in about 60,000 British casualties on the first day alone.

q.t: At what time and on what date did the First World War end?
q.e: The First World War ended at 11.00 am on 11th November 1918 with victory for Britain and its allies.

q.t: What was the Easter Rising of 1916?
q.e: Irish Nationalists were not willing to wait and in 1916 there was an uprising, the Easter Rising, against the British in Dublin. The leaders of the uprising were executed under military law. A guerrilla war against the British army and the police in Ireland followed.
o: An uprising against the British in Dublin
A strike by Irish farm workers

q.t: In 1922 Ireland became two countries. What were they called?
q.e: In 1921 a peace treaty was signed and in 1922 Ireland became two countries. The six counties in the north which were mainly Protestant remained part of the UK under the name Northern Ireland. The rest of Ireland became the Irish Free State. It had its own government and became a republic in 1949.
o: Northern Ireland and the Irish Free State
Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland
Northern Ireland and Eire Free State

q.t: How many counties in the north of Ireland remained part of the UK?
q.e: The six counties in the north which were mainly Protestant remained part of the UK under the name Northern Ireland.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: The BBC started radio broadcasts in 1922 and began the world's first regular television service in 1936. The television was developed by Scotsman John Logie Baird, and in 1932 he made the first television broadcast between London and Glasgow.
o: The BBC began the world's first regular television service in 1936
The BBC began the world's first regular television service in 1922

q.t: By roughly how much did car ownership change between 1930 and 1939?
q.e: As prices generally fell, those in work had more money to spend. Car ownership doubled from 1 million to 2 million between 1930 and 1939. In addition, many new houses were built.
o: It doubled, from 1 million to 2 million
It halved, from 2 million to 1 million
It rose from 1 million to 10 million

q.t: Which TWO writers are named in the handbook as prominent in the inter-war cultural blossoming?
q.e: It was also a time of cultural blossoming, with writers such as Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh prominent. The economist John Maynard Keynes published influential new theories of economics.

q.t: What event led Britain and France to declare war in 1939?
q.e: The British government tried to avoid another war. However, when Hitler invaded Poland in 1939, Britain and France declared war in order to stop his aggression.
o: The German invasion of the Soviet Union

q.t: How many men were rescued from the beaches around Dunkirk?
q.e: Many civilian volunteers in small pleasure and fishing boats from Britain helped the Navy to rescue more than 300,000 men from the beaches around Dunkirk. The evacuation gave rise to the phrase 'the Dunkirk spirit'.

q.t: Which TWO planes were the most important used by the Royal Air Force in the Battle of Britain?
q.e: The most important planes used by the Royal Air Force in the Battle of Britain were the Spitfire and the Hurricane, which were designed and built in Britain.

q.t: Which city was almost totally destroyed during the Blitz?
q.e: Despite this crucial victory, the German air force was able to continue bombing London and other British cities at night-time. This was called the Blitz. Coventry was almost totally destroyed and a great deal of damage was done in other cities, especially in the East End of London.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Churchill's speech to the House of Commons during the Battle of Britain included the line 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few'. His first speech as Prime Minister in 1940 included 'I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat'.
o: 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few' was said during the Battle of Britain
'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few' was said after Dunkirk

q.t: In which year was Winston Churchill voted the greatest Briton of all time by the public?
q.e: Following his death in 1965, Churchill was given a state funeral. He remains a much-admired figure to this day, and in 2002 was voted the greatest Briton of all time by the public.

q.t: On what date did allied forces land in Normandy?
q.e: On 6 June 1944, allied forces landed in Normandy, an event often referred to as 'D-Day'. Following victory on the beaches of Normandy, the allied forces pressed on through France and eventually into Germany.

q.t: Which TWO Japanese cities did the United States drop atom bombs on in August 1945?
q.e: The war against Japan ended in August 1945 when the United States dropped its newly developed atom bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

q.t: Which scientist led the British team that first split the atom?
q.e: Scientists led by Ernest Rutherford, working at Manchester and then Cambridge University, were the first to 'split the atom' and took part in the Manhattan Project in the United States, which developed the atomic bomb.

q.t: What did Alexander Fleming discover in 1928, and what was he researching at the time?
q.e: Born in Scotland, Fleming moved to London as a teenager and later qualified as a doctor. He was researching influenza, the 'flu', in 1928 when he discovered penicillin. Fleming won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945.

q.t: Which TWO scientists developed penicillin into a usable drug?
q.e: He was researching influenza in 1928 when he discovered penicillin. This was then further developed into a usable drug by the scientists Howard Florey and Ernst Chain. By the 1940s it was in mass production.

q.t: What is the pledge made by new citizens at a citizenship ceremony based on?
q.e: British society is founded on fundamental values and principles which all those living in the UK should respect and support. As part of the citizenship ceremony, new citizens pledge to uphold these values, giving loyalty to the United Kingdom and respecting its rights and freedoms.
o: The fundamental values and principles of British society

q.t: On what are the values reflected in British citizenship based, according to the handbook?
q.e: These values are reflected in the responsibilities, rights and privileges of being a British citizen or permanent resident of the UK. They are based on history and traditions and are protected by law, customs and expectations.
o: History and traditions, protected by law, customs and expectations
The rules of the Church of England
